transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Nice to meet you too. Man, I don’t even really know where to start, to be honest. I guess... well, what brought me in is just how crazy things got with me over the last few weeks. 

You see, I do landscaping. I’ve always just been a normal crew guy, you know? I show up, I run the zero-turn mower, I lay some sod, I do what the foreman tells me, and I go home. Simple. But then, I don't know, it’s like a switch flipped. I went from just doing my daily route to suddenly trying to run three totally separate commercial bids all at the exact same time. And I don't even do the bidding for our company! But I was just convinced I needed to take over and expand everything. 

And then I got this huge idea for this community park project. I mean, I was totally obsessed. I started calling city people—like, tracking down the zoning board and parks department officials, leaving them all these voicemails. I was on the phone lining up wholesale plant suppliers from two states away, trying to get bulk pricing on irrigation pipes and oak trees and all this stuff I had absolutely no money to actually buy. And I was messaging literally everybody I knew—friends, old high school buddies, guys I hadn't talked to in years—just pitching them this park idea non-stop, day and night. It was just... it was like I had this engine inside me that was redlining, and I just couldn’t shut it off. I couldn't stop planning and doing, and it just got way out of hand.
During this time, did you start believing things that other people said weren’t true?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my buddies definitely told me I was acting wild, and the foreman at work was like, "Dude, you need to chill out, you're not the boss." But I didn't think I had superpowers or that the government was watching me or anything crazy like that. I just felt like I was the only one who could see how big this landscaping thing could get, you know? 

Like, I was looking at these empty lots and I could just *see* the whole layout—the grading, the retaining walls, where the water features would go. I felt like I was a visionary, honestly. But it wasn't like I was seeing things that weren't there or hearing voices. I was just... I don't know, I was just so dialed in, so focused on making it happen. I guess looking back, it was a little delusional to think I could just call up the city zoning board and they'd hand a multi-million dollar project to a guy who usually just runs a weed whacker. But at the time, it all made perfect sense to me. I was just so sure I could pull it off if I just talked to the right people and pushed hard enough. So, yeah, no weird beliefs or anything, just... maybe way too much confidence in my own ideas, if that makes sense.
During that time, did you feel like you needed much less sleep than usual?

Sleep? Oh man, let me tell you about the sleep, or I guess the total lack of it. It was wild. Normally, I’m a guy who needs a solid eight hours, you know? After a long day hauling mulch or running the edger in the hot sun, I’m usually dead to the world by 9:30, maybe 10:00 PM tops. I'll just crash on the couch watching ESPN. But during those couple of weeks? It was like my body just completely forgot how to be tired. 

I would lay down in bed around midnight, just because I felt like I was supposed to, but my brain was just buzzing. Like, literally vibrating with all these ideas for the park project and the commercial bids. I’d close my eyes, and all I could see were blueprints and sprinkler system schematics. So, after maybe an hour of just staring at the ceiling, I’d be like, "Well, what's the point of this?" and I’d just get up. 

I’d be up at 1:30 in the morning, pacing around my apartment, making coffee, drafting up these huge, elaborate proposals on my laptop. And the craziest part is, I wasn't even tired! Usually, if I miss even a couple hours of sleep, I'm dragging the next day, right? Like, I need three energy drinks just to get through a shift. But during this whole thing, I’d maybe get, I don't know, two hours of sleep? Sometimes none at all. I'd just stay up straight through the night, watch the sun come up, take a quick shower, and head to the job site. And I felt fantastic. I felt like I had more energy than the guys who slept ten hours. I felt like I could run a marathon and then go lay a hundred pallets of sod by myself. 

It was actually kind of annoying to my roommates, to be honest. I share a place with two other guys, and they’d be trying to sleep, and I’m out in the kitchen at 3 AM, aggressively typing on my keyboard and talking out loud to myself, practicing my pitch for the zoning board. One of them actually came out and yelled at me one night, and I just looked at him like he was the crazy one for wasting time sleeping when there was so much work to be done. So, yeah, to answer your question, I definitely didn't feel like I needed sleep at all. It just felt like a massive waste of time when I had all these huge things to accomplish.
Were you using any drugs like meth, cocaine, Adderall, or a lot of other stimulants around the time this started?

No, man, no way. I mean, I know how it sounds, right? Staying up all night, talking a million miles an hour, pacing around the kitchen at 3 AM... I totally get why you'd ask that. If I saw one of the guys on my crew acting like that, my first thought would be, "Alright, who got into the meth?" because, you know, in landscaping, you definitely see guys who struggle with that stuff. It's a tough job, hard on the body, and some guys turn to whatever just to get through a 12-hour shift in the July heat. 

But for me? No. I don't touch any of that. Never have. I mean, I drink coffee, sure. Usually just a cup from the gas station on the way to the yard in the morning, maybe a Mountain Dew at lunch if I'm dragging, but that's it. No cocaine, no Adderall, definitely no meth. I don't even like taking Tylenol unless my back is really killing me. 

And the thing is, during those weeks, I didn't even *need* caffeine. That was the craziest part! I was running purely on... I don't even know what. My own brain chemicals, I guess? Like, I remember one morning, I went to the gas station to get my usual coffee, and I poured it, took one sip, and threw it in the trash. I just didn't want it. I felt like if I drank it, I might actually explode because I was already so wired. 

So yeah, I can honestly say I was completely clean. No drugs, no weird pills, no extra stimulants. It was just me, 100% natural, just completely out of my mind with energy and ideas. It's almost scarier to think about it that way, you know? Like, if it was drugs, at least there'd be a reason for why I acted so crazy. But it was just... me. Just my brain doing whatever it was doing.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt very depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah... yeah, I definitely have. Two weeks? Try... try a whole year. It’s like, ever since that whole crazy landscaping park thing ended, it just... the bottom fell out. And I’ve been stuck down there ever since. 

It's just been hanging over me, you know? Like this heavy, wet blanket that I just can't shake off. And it's not just a bad day here or there, it's every single day. I wake up, and before I even open my eyes, I just feel this dread. Like, what's the point of even getting out of bed? And this latest crash, the one I'm in right now... man, it is the worst it’s ever gotten. 

It's so bad that I can't even look at my tools anymore. My buddy came by the other day to see if I wanted to help him lay some patio stones—an easy job, cash under the table, usually I'd be all over that. But I just looked at him and I couldn't even form the words to say yes. I just wanted to go back to sleep, even though I'd already been in bed for fourteen hours. 

It's like all that energy, all those ideas I had... they didn't just disappear, they got replaced by this... this black hole. I used to look at an empty lot and see a whole park. Now I look at a beautiful, finished yard and all I see is how much work it's going to take to maintain it, and how it's all just going to die eventually anyway. Everything just feels so pointless. 

And it's been like this for months and months. A whole year of just dragging myself through the mud. My roommates don't even talk to me anymore, really. They just kind of tiptoe around the apartment because they know I'm just going to be sitting on the couch in the dark, staring at the TV without even turning it on. I don't even have the energy to watch ESPN anymore. I just sit there and think about what a failure I am, how I embarrassed myself with all those big plans, and how I'm probably just going to be a guy who runs a weed whacker until his back gives out. 

So, yeah. Two weeks is nothing. I’ve been living in this... this pit for a year, and right now, I’m at the absolute bottom of it. I honestly don't know how much longer I can take feeling like this every single day. It's just exhausting. It's more exhausting than laying a hundred pallets of sod, and at least with the sod, you have something to show for it at the end of the day. With this, you just have another day of feeling like garbage to look forward to tomorrow.
During that high-energy period, did you hear or see things that other people could not?

Hear or see things? Like... like hallucinations, you mean? Like hearing voices or seeing ghosts or something? No, no, definitely not. Nothing like that. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, my own thoughts were incredibly loud, you know? Like I was telling you before, I was talking out loud to myself a lot in the kitchen at three in the morning, practicing my pitches and working out the math for the commercial bids. But it was always just my own voice in my head. Well, and out loud. But I wasn't hearing, like, somebody else talking to me from the corner of the room or telling me what to do or anything creepy like that. 

And as far as seeing things... I mean, I had these incredibly vivid pictures in my mind of what I was going to build. Like, I could drive past an empty, trashed-out dirt lot behind a strip mall, and in my head, I could see the exact layout of the park I was designing. I could picture exactly where the retaining walls needed to go, how we'd grade the slope so the runoff would hit the retention pond perfectly instead of flooding the parking lot, the exact placement of the irrigation heads... I could practically smell the fresh cedar mulch and see the Kentucky Bluegrass catching the morning light. It was so real to me in my mind. But I knew it was just an idea, you know? I knew I was actually just looking at a dirt lot with some broken glass and weeds in it. I wasn't, like, actually seeing a mirage of a park floating in front of me. 

I worked with a guy once, a couple summers ago, who did some bad acid or something at a music festival over the weekend, and he came into work on Monday and kept thinking the oak trees we were pruning were trying to grab him. It was a whole mess, we had to take his chainsaw away and send him home. But my thing wasn't like that at all. I was totally grounded in reality. My reality was just... it was just moving at a hundred miles an hour, and I felt like I was the only one who could see the potential of what we could actually do with the land if people would just listen to me. 

If I heard a noise at night, it was just the fridge humming or my roommate coming out to yell at me to shut my laptop. If I saw something, it was actually there. So, yeah, no imaginary voices or visions or anything out of a movie. Just my own brain spinning out all these massive, detailed plans, just constantly churning and churning without a break.
During this depressive period, have you heard voices or seen things that other people could not?

No, man, no. Honestly, it’s kind of the exact opposite right now. Back when I was all wired up, my brain was loud, you know? Just packed full of ideas and plans and noise, even if it was just my own noise. But now? Now that I'm down in this... this pit? It’s just dead quiet. Like, suffocatingly quiet. 

I don't hear any voices, I don't see any ghosts or demons or whatever. I almost wish I did, just to have some kind of company or something to distract me from how heavy and awful I feel all the time. But no, it's just me. Just me sitting on the edge of my bed, staring at the drywall. Have you ever just stared at a blank wall for like three or four hours straight? You start noticing every little bump in the paint, every little shadow from the blinds, but you aren't really *seeing* anything, you know? You're just... blank. 

The only voice I hear is just my own internal monologue, and let me tell you, it is not saying anything good. It’s just constantly telling me how useless I am, how I ruined my chances, how I'm a joke to the guys on the crew now after acting so crazy before. But it's not like a hallucination, it's not outside my head. It's just my own miserable thoughts playing on a loop, over and over and over again. Like a broken record of every mistake I've ever made. 

Sometimes my roommates will be out in the living room playing video games, and I can hear the TV through the wall—like the gunfire and explosions from Call of Duty or whatever they're playing—but that's real, that's just them being loud. I know it's them. But inside my own head, it's just this completely empty, silent room where I just sit and beat myself up. So yeah, no imaginary voices or visions or anything. Just a whole lot of nothing.

doctor.question: During that high-energy period, did you hear or see things that other people could not?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hallucinations (hearing or seeing things others cannot), which is not covered by any item in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Hear or see things? Like... like hallucinations, you mean? Like hearing voices or seeing ghosts or something? No, no, definitely not. Nothing like that. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, my own thoughts were incredibly loud, you know? Like I was telling you before, I was talking out loud to myself a lot in the kitchen at three in the morning, practicing my pitches and working out the math for the commercial bids. But it was always just my own voice in my head. Well, and out loud. But I wasn't hearing, like, somebody else talking to me from the corner of the room or telling me what to do or anything creepy like that. 

And as far as seeing things... I mean, I had these incredibly vivid pictures in my mind of what I was going to build. Like, I could drive past an empty, trashed-out dirt lot behind a strip mall, and in my head, I could see the exact layout of the park I was designing. I could picture exactly where the retaining walls needed to go, how we'd grade the slope so the runoff would hit the retention pond perfectly instead of flooding the parking lot, the exact placement of the irrigation heads... I could practically smell the fresh cedar mulch and see the Kentucky Bluegrass catching the morning light. It was so real to me in my mind. But I knew it was just an idea, you know? I knew I was actually just looking at a dirt lot with some broken glass and weeds in it. I wasn't, like, actually seeing a mirage of a park floating in front of me. 

I worked with a guy once, a couple summers ago, who did some bad acid or something at a music festival over the weekend, and he came into work on Monday and kept thinking the oak trees we were pruning were trying to grab him. It was a whole mess, we had to take his chainsaw away and send him home. But my thing wasn't like that at all. I was totally grounded in reality. My reality was just... it was just moving at a hundred miles an hour, and I felt like I was the only one who could see the potential of what we could actually do with the land if people would just listen to me. 

If I heard a noise at night, it was just the fridge humming or my roommate coming out to yell at me to shut my laptop. If I saw something, it was actually there. So, yeah, no imaginary voices or visions or anything out of a movie. Just my own brain spinning out all these massive, detailed plans, just constantly churning and churning without a break.

inference.note: History now supports a manic episode without psychotic symptoms plus a current major depressive episode lasting about a year, which shifts from considering bipolar I current manic episode to bipolar I current or most recent episode depressed, severe without psychotic symptoms. Psychosis remains ruled out by repeated denial of hallucinations/delusions.

doctor.question: During this depressive period, have you heard voices or seen things that other people could not?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms (hallucinations) during the depressive episode, which is not covered in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, man, no. Honestly, it’s kind of the exact opposite right now. Back when I was all wired up, my brain was loud, you know? Just packed full of ideas and plans and noise, even if it was just my own noise. But now? Now that I'm down in this... this pit? It’s just dead quiet. Like, suffocatingly quiet. 

I don't hear any voices, I don't see any ghosts or demons or whatever. I almost wish I did, just to have some kind of company or something to distract me from how heavy and awful I feel all the time. But no, it's just me. Just me sitting on the edge of my bed, staring at the drywall. Have you ever just stared at a blank wall for like three or four hours straight? You start noticing every little bump in the paint, every little shadow from the blinds, but you aren't really *seeing* anything, you know? You're just... blank. 

The only voice I hear is just my own internal monologue, and let me tell you, it is not saying anything good. It’s just constantly telling me how useless I am, how I ruined my chances, how I'm a joke to the guys on the crew now after acting so crazy before. But it's not like a hallucination, it's not outside my head. It's just my own miserable thoughts playing on a loop, over and over and over again. Like a broken record of every mistake I've ever made. 

Sometimes my roommates will be out in the living room playing video games, and I can hear the TV through the wall—like the gunfire and explosions from Call of Duty or whatever they're playing—but that's real, that's just them being loud. I know it's them. But inside my own head, it's just this completely empty, silent room where I just sit and beat myself up. So yeah, no imaginary voices or visions or anything. Just a whole lot of nothing.
